steep/walk: Walk along this curve from left to right. Near the bottom it is almost flat, and farther right it climbs harder and harder.
steep/ask: So how steep is it at one exact point? Call the position across x, and take the point where x is one.
steep/tangent: Lay a straight edge on the curve there, so that it just touches. That line is the tangent, from the Latin for touching, and its tilt is what we want.
steep/leibniz: In 1684, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz published the first paper on calculus. Its title promised a new method for tangents.
steep/line: Start where steepness is easy: a straight line. You know one from school as y equals m x plus b, where m is its slope.
steep/two: Take y equals two x plus one. Each step of one to the right, it rises by two, so m is two.
steep/run: That is rise over run: how far up, divided by how far across. Over a run of two it rises four, and four over two is still two.
steep/shift: Make b minus two: two x minus two sits lower, but tilts the same, slope two. b only sets the height.
steep/fall: A line that falls has a negative slope. Four minus three x drops three for each step: slope minus three, the number multiplying x.
steep/forms: Whatever the form, find that number. Multiply out three times, x minus one, and you get three x minus three: slope three.
steep/half: And half of two x plus four is x plus two: slope one.
steep/curve: A curve has no single m: its tilt changes as you go. And rise over run needs two points, while a tangent touches at only one.
two/f: So name the curve. A function is a rule that turns each input into one output. Call this one f: its output for the input x is written f of x.
two/sq: This curve is f of x equals x squared: x times itself. So f of two is four.
two/h: For a second point, step to the right by a distance called h. With x at one and h of one, the second point is at two.
two/rise: Between them, f goes from one up to four. The rise is the later value minus the earlier one: three.
two/flip: Subtract the other way round, and you get minus three, as if the curve fell. The order matters.
two/slope: Over a run of one, the slope between the two points is three over one: three.
two/secant: The line through both points has that slope. It is called a secant, from the Latin for cutting, because it cuts through the curve.
two/formula: For any x and any step h, the slope between x and x plus h is f of x plus h, minus f of x, all over h.
shrink/pin: But three belongs to the whole stretch from one to two, and at one itself the curve is gentler. So slide the second point in: shrink h.
shrink/half: With h a half, the slope is two point five.
shrink/tenth: With h a tenth, it is two point one.
shrink/tiny: A hundredth gives two point zero one, and a thousandth, two point zero zero one. The slopes close in on two.
shrink/zero: Why not set h to zero? Then the rise and the run are both zero, and zero over zero has no answer. In code, it is an error.
shrink/limit: Instead, let h shrink toward zero without ever reaching it, and take the value the slopes close in on. It is called the limit: here, two.
shrink/derived: That limit is the derivative of f at one. The name is Joseph-Louis Lagrange's, from 1797: a function derived from f, giving its slope.
shrink/prime: He marked it with a tick, read prime: f prime of one equals two.
shrink/cauchy: In 1823, Augustin-Louis Cauchy defined it exactly this way: the limit of rise over run, as the two shrink toward zero together.
shrink/tangent: And the secant has become the tangent: through the point, with slope two, just touching the curve.
shrink/line: On a straight line every step gives the same slope, so for f of x equals three x minus one, the derivative is three at every x.
shrink/height: At x equals two, f prime of two is three. And f of two is five, but that is the line's height there, not its slope.
